home.pipelineLead: Same shape every time. Your app keeps its code path, the agent hangs off the edge, and every call has a way to fail back.

pipeline.appNote: Laravel, PrestaShop — whatever is already taking orders. No core overrides, no rewrite.
pipeline.cacheNote: Hit means no model call. This is where the 80% saving comes from.
pipeline.modelNote: Typed call, cost budget, timeout, retry.
pipeline.evalNote: Scored against fixtures. A regression does not ship.
pipeline.backNote: Behind a flag. Any failure falls back to the original path and nobody notices.

about.title: I have been shipping web software for eight years. The AI part is recent, and deliberate.
about.lead: I am a fullstack developer working in French and English, from the EU. Most of my career has been e-commerce backends — the unglamorous kind that has to survive Black Friday. Since Claude got good enough to trust with real work, I have been putting agents into those same systems.
about.story: Most "add AI" projects fail the same way: someone ships a prompt, nothing visibly breaks, and it quietly degrades for weeks. So I treat prompts like code that can regress. Fixture-based evals with tolerance bands, run on every prompt change and every model update. A cost budget before the first call. And insertion points chosen because they pay off, not because they demo well.|The e-commerce years taught me the other half. When a store is taking orders, you do not get to rewrite it. You add capability at the edges, behind a flag, with a way back. That constraint is why my AI work looks the way it does.

about.principlesLabel: What I believe about shipping AI
about.principles: An LLM feature without an eval harness is an outage you have not noticed yet.|Prompt caching is the cheapest ten-times win available. Do it before you optimise anything else.|Pick the insertion point by ROI, not by demo value. Support triage beats a chatbot.|If it cannot be rolled back behind a flag, it is not ready for a store that is taking orders.
